title: Partnership accounts
subject: Accountancy
summary: A partnership is a business owned by two or more persons who share profits and losses according to an agreement.
points: The profit sharing ratio is set in the partnership deed; without a deed profits are shared equally.
Partners' capital accounts may be fixed or fluctuating.
Interest on capital, drawings, salary and commission are adjusted before dividing profit.
Admission, retirement and death of a partner require revaluation of assets and goodwill adjustment.
Goodwill is compensated to the sacrificing partners.
example: A and B share 3:2; C is admitted for 1/5, so A and B sacrifice in their old ratio 3:2.
mistakes: Splitting profit equally when a deed exists.
Ignoring the sacrificing ratio when admitting a partner.

title: Company accounts: shares and debentures
subject: Accountancy
summary: Companies raise capital by issuing shares and borrow by issuing debentures.
points: Share capital is recorded as authorised, issued, subscribed and paid-up capital.
Shares may be issued at par, at premium or at a discount (now restricted).
Oversubscription is handled by pro-rata allotment, rejection or a combination.
Debentures carry fixed interest and are a liability, unlike shares.
Forfeiture of shares cancels the allotment when calls are unpaid.
example: A share of face value ₹10 issued at ₹12 creates a securities premium of ₹2 per share.
mistakes: Treating debenture interest as an appropriation of profit.
Recording premium as revenue income.

title: Cash flow statement
subject: Accountancy
summary: A cash flow statement explains changes in cash by classifying flows into operating, investing and financing activities.
points: Operating activities cover cash from core business operations.
Investing activities cover purchase and sale of fixed assets and investments.
Financing activities cover share capital, loans, dividends and interest paid.
Non-cash items such as depreciation are added back to net profit.
The statement reconciles opening and closing cash and bank balances.

formulas.name: Cash from operations
formulas.expr: net profit before tax + non-cash expenses − working capital increase

example: Depreciation of ₹50,000 is added back because it reduced profit without using cash.
mistakes: Classifying dividend paid as operating.
Forgetting to adjust for changes in working capital.

title: Rectification of errors and bank reconciliation
subject: Accountancy
summary: Errors in books are corrected through journal entries, and a bank reconciliation statement explains differences between cash book and passbook.
points: Errors of omission, commission, principle and compensating errors affect the trial balance differently.
One-sided errors are corrected in the affected account; two-sided errors need a journal entry.
A suspense account temporarily balances a trial balance with one-sided errors.
Bank reconciliation starts from the cash book or passbook balance and adjusts for cheques, charges and direct deposits.
Timing differences are not errors and need no journal entry.

formulas.name: Reconciliation
formulas.expr: cash book balance ± adjustments = passbook balance

example: A cheque deposited but not yet cleared reduces the passbook balance compared with the cash book.
mistakes: Recording timing differences as errors.
Correcting a one-sided error with a two-sided entry.

title: Bills of exchange and inventory valuation
subject: Accountancy
summary: Bills of exchange are credit instruments, and inventory is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.
points: A bill of exchange is a written order to pay a sum on a date.
The drawer, drawee and payee are the parties; endorsement transfers the bill.
Dishonour of a bill is recorded with noting charges.
Inventory valuation follows the lower of cost and net realisable value.
Cost may be found by FIFO, weighted average or specific identification.

formulas.name: Net realisable value
formulas.expr: expected selling price − estimated costs to complete and sell

formulas.name: Closing inventory
formulas.expr: opening inventory + purchases − cost of goods sold

example: Goods costing ₹10,000 now sell for ₹8,000, so inventory is valued at ₹8,000.
mistakes: Valuing inventory at selling price without deducting costs.
Forgetting noting charges on dishonour.

title: Business environment
subject: Business Studies
summary: The business environment is the set of external forces — economic, social, technological, political and legal — that affect a firm.
points: The environment offers opportunities and threats that a firm must scan.
Dimensions include economic, social, technological, political and legal conditions.
Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation reshaped Indian business after 1991.
Environmental scanning helps planning, policy making and early warning.
example: A new pollution norm is a legal environment change that forces factories to upgrade equipment.
mistakes: Treating the environment as only economic.
Ignoring legal changes in planning.

title: Planning and organising
subject: Business Studies
summary: Planning sets objectives and courses of action; organising arranges resources and authority to carry them out.
points: Planning is primary, continuous and future-oriented, and it reduces uncertainty.
A plan needs objectives, strategies, policies, procedures and rules.
Organising divides work, assigns duties and establishes reporting relationships.
Delegation transfers authority; decentralisation spreads decision making.
Span of control and departmentation shape the organisation structure.
example: A firm creates separate production and marketing departments, which is departmentation by function.
mistakes: Confusing delegation with decentralisation.
Thinking planning guarantees success.

title: Staffing, directing and controlling
subject: Business Studies
summary: Staffing fills positions with the right people, directing guides them, and controlling checks performance against standards.
points: Staffing includes recruitment, selection, training and appraisal.
Directing involves supervision, motivation, leadership and communication.
Maslow's hierarchy and other theories explain motivation.
Controlling sets standards, measures performance and takes corrective action.
Management by exception focuses attention on significant deviations.
example: A sales target of 100 units per month with a variance report is an example of the control process.
mistakes: Treating control as punishment.
Confusing recruitment with selection.

title: Financial management and financial markets
subject: Business Studies
summary: Financial management decides how much to raise, from where, and how to use funds, while financial markets channel savings to investors.
points: Financing, investment and dividend decisions are the three financial decisions.
Capital structure mixes debt and equity; too much debt raises financial risk.
Working capital is the funds needed for day-to-day operations.
The primary market issues new securities; the secondary market trades existing ones.
SEBI regulates the securities market to protect investors.
example: A company raising money through an IPO is operating in the primary market.
mistakes: Confusing the primary and secondary markets.
Ignoring the risk of high debt.

title: Marketing mix and consumer protection
subject: Business Studies
summary: Marketing mixes product, price, place and promotion, and consumer law protects buyers from unfair trade.
points: The marketing mix is the four Ps: product, price, place and promotion.
Branding, labelling and packaging support product positioning.
Pricing methods include cost plus, penetration and skimming.
Channels of distribution move goods from producer to consumer.
The Consumer Protection Act 2019 gives redressal commissions and e-commerce rights.
example: A new phone launched at a low price to gain market share uses penetration pricing.
mistakes: Treating marketing as only advertising.
Forgetting that the Act covers e-commerce.

title: Government budget and the economy
subject: Economics
summary: A government budget is an annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure, used to influence the economy.
points: Revenue receipts are not matched by a liability or asset reduction; capital receipts are.
Revenue expenditure does not create assets; capital expenditure does.
A fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
Deficits may be financed by borrowing, which adds to public debt.
Fiscal policy can stabilise demand during booms and recessions.

formulas.name: Fiscal deficit
formulas.expr: total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts)

example: If expenditure is ₹50 lakh crore and receipts ₹45 lakh crore, the fiscal deficit is ₹5 lakh crore.
mistakes: Confusing fiscal and revenue deficit.
Treating borrowing as a receipt without consequence.

title: Balance of payments and exchange rate
subject: Economics
summary: The balance of payments records a country's transactions with the rest of the world, and the exchange rate links its currency to others.
points: The current account covers goods, services and transfers; the capital account covers assets and liabilities.
A current account deficit must be financed by capital inflows or reserves.
A devaluation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer.
Exchange rates may be fixed or floating.
Depreciation of a currency can improve the trade balance over time if demand is elastic.

formulas.name: Current account balance
formulas.expr: exports of goods and services − imports + net transfers

example: A rise in crude oil imports widens India's current account deficit.
mistakes: Saying the balance of payments can be in permanent surplus.
Confusing devaluation with depreciation.

title: Inflation and unemployment
subject: Economics
summary: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, and unemployment is the share of the labour force without work.
points: Demand-pull inflation comes from excess demand; cost-push from rising input costs.
Inflation redistributes income away from fixed-income earners.
The Phillips curve suggests a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
Types of unemployment include frictional, structural, cyclical and seasonal.
Monetary and fiscal policy are used to manage demand.
example: A 6% inflation rate means a basket costing ₹100 last year costs about ₹106 now.
mistakes: Calling a one-time price rise inflation.
Counting people outside the labour force as unemployed.

title: Indian economy 1950–90 and economic reforms
subject: Economics
summary: India mixed planning with public investment after independence, then liberalised in 1991 after a balance-of-payments crisis.
points: The Five Year Plans set targets for agriculture and industry.
The Green Revolution raised wheat and rice output.
The licence-permit system regulated industry and limited competition.
The 1991 reforms liberalised trade, privatised some public units and opened foreign investment.
Growth rose but agriculture and employment did not keep pace evenly.
example: The 1991 rupee devaluation and removal of industrial licensing marked the reform turn.
mistakes: Treating reforms as a single policy.
Assuming the Green Revolution covered all crops equally.

title: Human capital, rural development and employment
subject: Economics
summary: Investment in education and health builds human capital, and rural development covers credit, infrastructure and employment schemes.
points: Human capital formation raises productivity and income.
Rural credit comes from formal sources (banks, cooperatives) and informal moneylenders.
MGNREGA guarantees rural wage employment.
Agricultural diversification and organic farming raise rural incomes.
Informal workers lack social security and job protection.
example: A village library and school raise literacy, which improves earning capacity over time.
mistakes: Confusing human capital with human development.
Ignoring informal employment in official statistics.

title: Python programming fundamentals
subject: Computer Science
summary: Python is a high-level language with simple syntax, used for scripting, data work and teaching programming.
points: Variables hold references to objects; types include int, float, str, list, tuple and dict.
Indentation defines blocks instead of braces.
Input from input() is a string and must be converted for arithmetic.
Operators include arithmetic, comparison, logical and membership operators.
Errors may be syntax, runtime or logical.

formulas.name: Integer division
formulas.expr: a // b gives the quotient, a % b the remainder

example: print(int(input('Number: ')) * 2) doubles the number typed by the user.
mistakes: Adding a string to an integer without converting.
Mixing tabs and spaces for indentation.

title: Conditional and iterative statements
subject: Computer Science
summary: Conditionals choose between paths and loops repeat statements, giving programs control over execution.
points: if, elif and else select a block based on conditions.
for loops iterate over a sequence; while loops repeat while a condition is true.
break exits a loop and continue skips to the next iteration.
Nested loops are used for patterns and tables.
Infinite loops occur when the condition never becomes false.
example: for i in range(1, 6): print(i) prints 1 to 5.
mistakes: Forgetting the colon after a condition.
Changing the loop variable inside a for loop expecting extra iterations.

title: Functions and modules
subject: Computer Science
summary: Functions group reusable code, and modules group functions into importable files.
points: A function is defined with def and may take parameters and return a value.
Arguments may be positional, keyword or default.
Local variables exist only inside a function; global variables are visible throughout.
Modules are imported with import or from ... import.
The standard library includes math, random, statistics and datetime.
example: def area(r): return 3.14 * r * r makes area(2) return 12.56.
mistakes: Thinking a function without return gives None is an error.
Modifying a global inside a function without global.

title: Lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries
subject: Computer Science
summary: Python's built-in collections store groups of values in different ways: ordered, immutable, unique or keyed.
points: Lists are ordered and mutable; tuples are ordered and immutable.
Sets store unique elements and support union, intersection and difference.
Dictionaries store key–value pairs with fast lookup by key.
Slicing extracts a part of a sequence with [start:stop:step].
List comprehensions build lists in one expression.
example: d = {'a': 1}; d['a'] returns 1, and d.get('b') returns None instead of an error.
mistakes: Trying to change a tuple.
Using a mutable list as a dictionary key.

title: File handling
subject: Computer Science
summary: Files store data permanently, and Python reads and writes them through file objects.
points: open() takes a filename and a mode: r, w, a, or b for binary.
write() writes strings; writelines() writes a list of strings.
read(), readline() and readlines() read different amounts of data.
The with statement closes the file automatically.
CSV files can be handled with the csv module.
example: with open('data.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('hello') creates the file and closes it safely.
mistakes: Opening in 'w' mode when you meant to append.
Forgetting to close a file or use with.

title: Database concepts and SQL
subject: Computer Science
summary: Relational databases store data in tables, and SQL queries, inserts and updates that data.
points: A relation is a table with rows (tuples) and columns (attributes).
Keys identify rows: primary key is unique, foreign key references another table.
DDL creates and alters structures; DML inserts, updates and deletes data.
SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and HAVING queries data.
Aggregate functions include COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX.

formulas.name: Select
formulas.expr: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition;

example: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 ORDER BY name; lists high scorers alphabetically.
mistakes: Using = instead of IS NULL for null checks.
Grouping without including the grouped column.

title: Computer networks
subject: Computer Science
summary: A network connects devices so they can share data and resources, using agreed protocols.
points: Topologies include star, bus, ring and mesh, each with different cost and reliability.
A LAN covers a small area; a WAN spans large distances.
The internet is a network of networks using TCP/IP.
IP addresses identify devices; DNS translates names into addresses.
Devices include hubs, switches, routers and modems.
example: A school computer lab is a LAN; connecting it to an ISP makes it part of a WAN.
mistakes: Calling the internet the same as the world wide web.
Confusing a hub with a switch.

title: Boolean algebra and logic gates
subject: Computer Science
summary: Boolean algebra uses true and false values, and logic gates implement its operations in hardware.
points: Basic gates are AND, OR and NOT; NAND and NOR are universal gates.
Truth tables list outputs for every input combination.
De Morgan's theorems convert between AND and OR forms.
Karnaugh maps simplify Boolean expressions.
Adders and flip-flops are built from gates.
example: A NAND gate gives 0 only when both inputs are 1.
mistakes: Treating NAND as AND followed by NOT on each input.
Forgetting that NOR is also universal.

title: Computer science and society
subject: Computer Science
summary: Computing raises questions of privacy, security, intellectual property, accessibility and the impact of automation.
points: Personal data must be collected with consent and protected from misuse.
Cybercrimes include phishing, identity theft, hacking and cyberbullying.
Software piracy violates copyright; open-source licences allow reuse under conditions.
Automation changes employment and requires new skills.
The digital divide limits access to technology for poorer and rural users.
example: A phishing email that imitates a bank steals login details if the link is clicked.
mistakes: Sharing passwords or OTPs with anyone.
Assuming free software is always unrestricted.

title: English grammar: tenses
subject: English
summary: Tense shows the time of an action and whether it is simple, continuous, perfect or perfect continuous.
points: Simple present describes habits and general truths; present continuous describes actions now.
Present perfect links a past action to the present; past perfect shows an earlier past.
Future forms include will, going to and present continuous for arrangements.
Time markers such as since, for, already and yesterday guide the choice of tense.
Sequence of tenses keeps the tense consistent in reported speech.
example: She has lived here since 2019 uses present perfect with 'since' for an action continuing to now.
mistakes: Using present perfect with a finished past time like yesterday.
Mixing 'since' and 'for'.

title: Active and passive voice; direct and indirect speech
subject: English
summary: Voice shows whether the subject acts or is acted upon, and narration reports speech directly or indirectly.
points: In passive voice the object becomes the subject and the verb becomes be + past participle.
Passive is used when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
In indirect speech pronouns, tense and time words shift unless the reporting verb is in the present.
Questions, commands and requests change structure when reported.
Said becomes told when an object follows.
example: She said, "I am tired." becomes She said that she was tired.
mistakes: Changing the tense when the reporting verb is present.
Forgetting to change 'today' to 'that day'.

title: Writing skills: letters, notices, reports, articles
subject: English
summary: Formal writing follows fixed formats: letters, notices, reports, articles, speeches and diary entries.
points: A formal letter has sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation, body and closing.
A notice is short, in a box, with a heading, date, and the writer's name and designation.
A report states what, where, when, who and why in past tense with a headline.
An article has an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion, with a title.
Word limits matter: stay within the range given in the question.
example: A notice for a lost water bottle names the item, place, date and where to return it.
mistakes: Writing a letter without a subject line.
Exceeding the word limit and losing marks.

title: Reading comprehension and note making
subject: English
summary: Comprehension tests whether you can find, infer and summarise information from a passage.
points: Read the questions first, then scan the passage for the relevant lines.
Answer in your own words where asked; do not copy whole sentences for 'in your own words' questions.
Inference questions need a conclusion from clues, not a direct quote.
Note making uses headings, sub-points and abbreviations.
Vocabulary questions test meaning in context, not dictionary definitions alone.
example: If a passage says a plan was 'shelved', the answer is postponed, not placed on a shelf.
mistakes: Lifting lines for a summary.
Ignoring the marks allotted per question.

title: Hindi vyakaran: kaarak, samas aur alankar
subject: Hindi
summary: Hindi grammar covers kaarak, samas, upasarg–pratyay, ras and alankar, which are tested in vyakaran sections.
points: There are eight kaarak; vibhakti markers such as ne, ko and se show the relation.
Samas joins two or more words into one; types include tatpurush, dwandwa, bahuvrihi and dwigu.
Upasarg change meaning and pratyay form new words.
Alankar are figures of speech: anupras, upama, rupak, utpreksha and yamak.
Ras are the nine aesthetic emotions evoked by literature.
example: 'Raja ka putra' becomes 'rajputra', an example of tatpurush samas.
mistakes: Confusing upama (simile) with rupak (metaphor).
Counting vibhakti as kaarak itself.

title: Hindi rachna: patra, nibandh aur anuchhed
subject: Hindi
summary: Hindi writing skills include patra-lekhan, nibandh, anuchhed, suchna and vigyapan.
points: Aupcharik patra follows a fixed format with sender, date, receiver, vishay and signature.
Anuchhed is a short, focused paragraph with one main idea.
Nibandh has a bhoomika, vistar and upasamhar.
Suchna is brief and factual; vigyapan uses persuasive short lines.
Language should be simple and free of spelling errors.
example: A leave-application patra begins with the sender's address, then date, receiver, vishay and body.
mistakes: Writing an aupcharik patra without a vishay line.
Making an anuchhed too long and unfocused.

title: Population geography
subject: Geography
summary: Population geography studies the distribution, density, growth and composition of population.
points: Population distribution is uneven and shaped by terrain, climate, soils and resources.
Density is people per square kilometre; growth comes from births, deaths and migration.
The demographic transition moves from high birth and death rates to low ones.
Population composition covers age, sex, literacy and occupation.
An ageing population raises dependency and health costs.
example: A country with birth rate 30 and death rate 8 per thousand grows naturally at 2.2% a year.
mistakes: Confusing growth rate with natural increase when migration is large.
Ignoring age structure when comparing countries.

title: Human development
subject: Geography
summary: Human development measures how far people can live long, healthy and knowledgeable lives.
points: The Human Development Index combines life expectancy, education and income.
Development is about capabilities and choices, not income alone.
The HDI ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better development.
Inequality-adjusted HDI and gender-related indices reveal gaps hidden by averages.
Bhutan's Gross National Happiness is an alternative measure.

formulas.name: HDI
formulas.expr: geometric mean of health, education and income indices

example: Two countries with the same income can have different HDI because health and schooling differ.
mistakes: Treating HDI as a pure income measure.
Comparing HDI across years without noting methodology changes.

title: Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary activities
subject: Geography
summary: Economic activities are grouped by what they take from nature, transform, service or research.
points: Primary activities directly use natural resources: farming, fishing, mining, forestry.
Secondary activities process raw materials: manufacturing, construction, power.
Tertiary activities provide services: trade, transport, banking, education.
Quaternary activities involve knowledge work such as research and computing.
Quinary activities involve top-level decision making.
example: Turning cotton into cloth is a secondary activity, while selling the cloth is tertiary.
mistakes: Classifying mining as secondary.
Ignoring that many workers hold jobs across sectors.

title: Transport, communication and international trade
subject: Geography
summary: Transport and communication move goods, people and information, and international trade exchanges them between countries.
points: Modes include road, rail, water, air and pipelines, each suited to different goods and distances.
Ports and terminals are gateways of international trade.
Trade may be bilateral or multilateral; balance of trade compares exports and imports.
Containerisation reduced handling costs and speeded up shipping.
Digital communication now carries services across borders.
example: Coal moves by rail and ship because it is bulky and low in value per tonne.
mistakes: Confusing balance of trade with balance of payments.
Assuming air transport suits bulky goods.

title: India: population, migration and settlements
subject: Geography
summary: India's population is unevenly distributed, shaped by migration and growing urban settlements.
points: The northern plains and coastal areas are densely populated; mountains and deserts are sparse.
Migration may be rural-to-rural, rural-to-urban or urban-to-urban.
Push factors include poverty and land pressure; pull factors include jobs and services.
Settlements are compact or dispersed, rural or urban.
Urbanisation brings slums, congestion and pressure on services.
example: Seasonal migration from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh to Punjab during harvest is rural-to-rural migration.
mistakes: Calling all movement of people urbanisation.
Ignoring seasonal and circular migration.
